mcqs.question: Why does LOOK scheduling serve all up-requests in floor order before reversing, instead of jumping to whichever request arrived first?
options: Passengers already being served in the current direction aren't skipped for a request that merely arrived earlier, and total travel distance for the request set drops compared to jumping around by arrival order
It guarantees the elevator never has to stop for the same floor twice
It removes the need for a direction-sorted queue
First-come-first-served ordering is prohibited by most building safety codes
mcqs.explanation: LOOK's benefit is efficiency and fairness for in-progress riders: serving in floor order along the current direction minimizes backtracking and doesn't strand passengers already being served. It doesn't prevent repeat stops, it actually relies on a direction-sorted queue rather than removing the need for one, and there's no such safety-code prohibition.

mcqs.question: Why is ScoringStrategy implemented as a pluggable interface that assignRequest calls, rather than writing the cost formula directly inside assignRequest?
options: It makes the controller communicate faster with each elevator
It removes the need for a per-elevator queue
Interfaces are required by Java whenever a method processes more than one object in a loop
Swapping in a different cost function — starvation-aware, load-balancing — becomes writing a new class instead of editing the dispatch loop itself
mcqs.explanation: The Strategy interface isolates 'how do we score an elevator' from 'how do we pick the best one,' so changing the scoring logic doesn't touch assignRequest at all. It has no effect on communication speed, doesn't remove the queue, and Java has no such interface requirement.

mcqs.question: A passenger double-taps floor 6, sending two near-simultaneous requests to the same elevator. What prevents floor 6 from being queued twice?
options: TreeSet automatically merges any two requests for the same floor regardless of timing
An idempotent request-id — floor, direction, and a dedup window — lets the controller recognize the second press as a duplicate of the first rather than a new request
The elevator's hardware physically cannot receive two requests within the same second
Double-presses are filtered out at the physical button level, not in software
mcqs.explanation: Deduping is a software concern solved by an idempotent request identity plus a time window, not an accident of the data structure or the hardware. TreeSet on its own doesn't know two adds represent the same logical event, and there's no such hardware guarantee.

mcqs.question: Why can 'always assign the nearest elevator by distance' cause a request to wait indefinitely in a busy building?
options: It can't — nearest-elevator assignment always completes every request within a fixed time
Because TreeSet-based queues degrade to O(n) lookup under high request volume
A far-away request keeps losing out to newer, closer requests as they keep arriving, since pure distance never grows worse for those newer requests, only for the one waiting
Because only one elevator is allowed to be assigned a new request per minute
mcqs.explanation: Starvation happens because distance-only scoring never accounts for how long a request has already waited, so a far request can be perpetually outbid by closer newcomers. There's no such fixed-time guarantee, this isn't a data-structure performance issue, and there's no per-minute assignment cap in the design.

mcqs.question: When does a centralized ElevatorController's global-optimization approach make more sense than having each elevator independently bid on requests?
options: When the controller can be treated as reliable, always-available infrastructure — centralizing lets the scoring function see the whole system's state at once, which decentralized bidding cannot
Always — decentralized bidding is strictly worse in every scenario
Only in buildings with fewer than three elevators
Only when every elevator in the building is a freight elevator
mcqs.explanation: The trade-off is optimality versus fault isolation: centralized scoring can weigh the whole system at once but becomes a single point of failure, which is a reasonable bet when the controller is solid infrastructure. Decentralized bidding has real advantages (fault isolation) so it isn't strictly worse, and neither approach is tied to elevator count or car type.
